steps.body:
Recent observations fail to confirm earlier ones that apparently showed a comet reservoir far out in our solar system (i.e. recent observations did not provide evidence of a comet reservoir far out in the solar system).
Professor B recognizes this and claims that this nonconfirmation is enough to show that earlier observations were incorrect.
pivot (But)
The recent observations occurred under poor conditions.
steps.label: Statements

steps.body:
We have to distinguish between factual claims and attributed opinions sometimes on Inference questions, but the first sentence is both.
Saying that "Professor Bums recognizes X" means both that X is true (according to the speaker, whose statements we are accepting as true) and that Professor Bums believes it.
There isn't any Conditional, Causal, or Mathematical wording in this paragraph but there is a Pivot. Typically, if a Most Supported paragraph ends with a Pivot sentence, the correct answer represents a safely worded way of resolving the tension created by the pivot word. We call that sort of pattern Reconcile the Pivot.
The tension here is that Professor Bums thinks that new observations refute old observations, but the speaker is pointing out that these new observations occurred under poor conditions.
This seems to suggest that the new data points aren't super trustworthy. Would we be a little hasty to toss out the old observations as invalid, based off some sketchy new observations?
steps.label: Evaluate

steps.body:
The wrong answers will probably go overboard and say, "Thus, the recent observations are worthless. Thus, we should still believe the earlier observations. Thus, there is a comet reservoir far out in the solar system."
But we want something much more moderate, like, "Thus, it may be hasty to deem to old observations as incorrect based on this somewhat questionable new data" or "Thus, we don't have a good grasp right now on whether or not evidence of a comet reservoir exists".
